meta.title: Planning and Reflection
meta.thesis: Planning lets an agent commit to a sequence of steps before acting; reflection lets it critique its own output and revise. Together they turn a reactive turn-by-turn loop into a goal-directed agent that catches its own mistakes.

mentalMap.title: Planning and Reflection: mental map
mentalMap.caption: Start with why these two loops exist, then open each block for the mechanism and where it breaks.
mentalMap.oneLineThesis: Planning commits an agent to a sequence before it acts; reflection critiques the result and revises — two control loops layered on the basic agent loop.

nodes.label: Why plan and reflect
nodes.sub: The failure of pure react-and-respond, and what these loops add.
nodes.orient: Why a reactive agent loop stalls on multi-step goals, and what planning plus reflection fix.
nodes.what: Frames the problem: a turn-by-turn agent has no commitment and no self-check, so it drifts and ships errors.
nodes.relevance: Without this framing, planning and reflection look like optional extras instead of answers to concrete failure modes.

nodes.label: How planning works
nodes.sub: Decompose the goal into steps before executing any of them.
nodes.orient: How an agent turns a goal into an ordered plan of subtasks before acting on the first one.
nodes.what: The planning mechanism: decomposition, ordering, and storing the plan so the agent can track progress.
nodes.relevance: Planning is what gives the agent foresight — it is the half of the pair that prevents aimless wandering.

nodes.label: How reflection works
nodes.sub: Critique the output, then decide to accept, retry, or replan.
nodes.orient: How an agent inspects its own result, scores it against the goal, and chooses to revise or stop.
nodes.what: The reflection mechanism: generate, critique against criteria, then revise — the self-correction loop.
nodes.relevance: Reflection is the half that catches errors the plan could not foresee, turning a draft into a checked answer.

nodes.sub: A minimal plan-execute-reflect loop you can read in one screen.
nodes.orient: How plan, execute, and reflect combine into one control loop with a bounded revision budget.
nodes.what: A tiny implementation that decomposes, executes step by step, reflects, and revises within a budget.
nodes.relevance: Seeing the loop in code makes the control flow — and where the budget guard goes — concrete.

nodes.label: Where it breaks
nodes.sub: Failure modes, the cost tradeoff, and a self-check.
nodes.orient: When planning and reflection backfire — stale plans, reflection loops, sycophantic self-critique — and how to bound them.
nodes.what: The late-module failure modes plus a decision on how much planning and reflection a task actually warrants.
nodes.relevance: Knowing the failure modes is what separates adding these loops blindly from using them where they pay off.

modules.title: Why plan and reflect
modules.sub: Starts the spine: the failures of a purely reactive agent.
modules.summary: A bare agent loop reacts one turn at a time with no commitment and no self-check. Planning adds foresight; reflection adds self-correction. This module names the concrete failures each one answers.
objectives: Explain the two failures of a purely reactive agent loop that planning and reflection address.
Distinguish planning (commit before acting) from reflection (critique after acting).
Name when adding these loops is worth the extra cost and latency.

blocks.title: The problem these loops solve

spans.text: Before reading on, predict:
what goes wrong when an agent decides each step only after seeing the previous result, with no plan and no review of its own output?
A bare
agent

runs a reactive loop: observe, decide one action, act, repeat. That is enough for short tasks, but it fails two ways on real goals. First, with no commitment to a sequence, the agent loses the thread on multi-step work — it re-derives the goal every turn and wanders. Second, with no review of its own output, a confident-but-wrong answer ships straight to the user.
Planning
answers the first failure: the agent decomposes the goal into an ordered sequence
before
acting, so each turn advances a known plan.
Reflection

answers the second: the agent critiques its own result against the goal and revises before committing. They are two distinct control loops layered on top of the basic agent loop — foresight and hindsight.

items.text: Reactive only: cheap and fast, but drifts on long goals and ships unchecked output.
Planning: commitment before action — fixes drift, costs an up-front planning call.
Reflection: critique after action — catches errors, costs one or more extra revision passes.

blocks.title: Click through the plan-execute-reflect loop
blocks.caption: Where planning and reflection sit relative to the basic act step.

steps.label: Plan
steps.detail: Decompose the goal into an ordered list of subtasks before any tool runs.

steps.label: Execute
steps.detail: Carry out the next step in the plan, usually a tool call, and capture the result.

steps.label: Reflect
steps.detail: Critique the result against the goal: is it correct, complete, and on-plan?

steps.label: Revise or advance
steps.detail: If the critique fails, retry or replan; if it passes, advance to the next step or finish.

stops.label: Reactive
stops.note: No plan, no reflection — one decision per turn.

stops.label: Plan-then-act
stops.note: Commit to a sequence, but trust each result.

stops.label: Plan + reflect
stops.note: Add a bounded self-critique loop on top of the plan.

blocks.title: Diagnose which loop a failure needs

spans.text: Did the agent wander off-goal or repeat work across turns, or did it confidently return a wrong answer? The first is a planning gap; the second is a reflection gap.
Drift and lost context call for planning — decompose and commit to a sequence. Unchecked, plausible-but-wrong output calls for reflection — add a critique pass before committing.
Both loops add model calls. Decide the budget up front: how many plan revisions and how many reflection passes a task is worth before it must ship or stop.

blocks.title: Concrete use case: a research-and-write agent

spans.text: An agent asked to "write a competitive brief on three vendors" fails reactively: it answers about one vendor, forgets the other two, and never checks coverage. With planning it commits to a four-step plan (research A, research B, research C, synthesize).

With reflection it then critiques the draft — "does this cover all three vendors and cite a source for each claim?" — and revises the gaps before returning. Planning kept it on-goal; reflection caught the missing citation.

blocks.title: Planning vs reflection in one table

spans.text: Planning runs once up front and writes a plan into
state

; reflection runs after each result and reads the goal plus the latest output. Planning is foresight over future steps; reflection is hindsight over the step just taken. They are independent — you can ship either alone — but they reinforce each other: reflection can trigger a replan.
Treat the plan as mutable state, not a fixed script: reflection's most powerful move is to invalidate a step and ask the planner to revise.

blocks.prompt: An agent keeps returning fluent answers that are subtly wrong, but it never loses track of the goal. Which loop does it need?

options.text: Planning — it needs to commit to a sequence of steps.
Reflection — it needs to critique and revise its own output before committing.
Neither — a larger model would fix it without changing the loop.

blocks.explanation: Staying on-goal means planning is not the gap; shipping confident-but-wrong output is exactly the failure reflection (self-critique then revise) addresses.

modules.title: How planning works
modules.sub: Follows m1: zoom into the foresight loop — decomposition.
modules.summary: Planning turns a goal into an ordered list of subtasks before execution. This module covers decomposition, the plan as mutable state, and the choice between planning once versus replanning as you go.
objectives: Describe how an agent decomposes a goal into an ordered plan.
Explain why the plan must live in state, not just in the prompt.
Choose between plan-once and interleaved replanning for a given task.

blocks.title: Decomposition: goal to ordered plan

spans.text: Planning starts with
decomposition
: the agent prompts the model to break a goal into an ordered list of subtasks, each small enough to map to a single
tool
call or short action. The output is a plan — a data structure, not prose — that the agent stores in
state
and walks through one step at a time.

Keeping the plan in state (not just in the conversation) is what lets the agent track which step it is on, mark steps done, and survive a context-window trim. The plan is the agent's working memory of intent.
There are two timing strategies:

items.text: Plan-once: build the whole plan up front, then execute. Cheap and predictable, but brittle if reality differs from the plan.
Interleaved replanning: plan a step, execute, then re-plan the remainder using the result. Robust to surprises, but costs a planning call per step.

blocks.title: Write a plan that the agent can execute

spans.text: Prompt the model to emit the plan as a list of steps with an id, a description, and the tool each step expects — so the runtime can index it, not just read it.

steps.label: Size each step to one action

spans.text: A step that needs three tool calls is two steps too big. Right-sized steps make progress legible and reflection (next module) able to score one thing at a time.
Persist the plan in state with a status per step. The agent reads the first unfinished step each turn — this is what keeps it from re-deriving the goal.

blocks.title: Concrete use case: plan-once vs replan

spans.text: Booking travel with fixed dates suits plan-once: search flights, search hotel, book both. The steps rarely surprise you. Debugging a failing test suite suits interleaved replanning: you cannot know step three until step two tells you which assertion broke.
The rule of thumb: plan-once when the environment is predictable; replan when each result reshapes what is possible next.

blocks.title: The plan is mutable state

spans.text: Represent the plan as a list of step records with status fields (pending, active, done, failed). The agent's turn becomes: read the active step, execute it, write back its status. Because the structure is data, reflection or replanning can rewrite remaining steps without touching completed ones.
Never bury the plan only inside the prompt history. If the context window is trimmed, an in-prompt-only plan vanishes; a plan in state survives.

blocks.prompt: Why store the plan in state rather than only in the conversation prompt?

options.text: State is faster for the model to read than the prompt.
A plan in state survives context trimming and lets the agent track per-step status reliably.
Putting the plan in state means you no longer need any tools.

blocks.explanation: The prompt history can be trimmed and offers no structured status; state gives the agent a durable, indexable record of which step is active.

modules.title: How reflection works
modules.sub: Follows m2: after the plan executes, critique the result.
modules.summary: Reflection is generate, then critique against criteria, then revise. This module covers what makes a critique useful, the strategies for it, and how to choose how much reflection a task warrants.
objectives: Explain the generate-critique-revise loop and what makes a critique signal useful.
Compare reflection strategies by quality gain, cost, and risk.
Choose how much reflection to apply based on the task's error cost.

blocks.title: Generate, critique, revise

spans.text: Before reading on, predict:
if an agent critiques its own work using the same model and the same prompt, what kind of error will it systematically miss?
Reflection is a three-beat loop:
generate
an output,
critique
it against explicit criteria, then
revise
based on the critique. The whole loop hinges on the critique producing a real signal — a specific, actionable judgement, not a vague "looks good."
A useful critique is grounded in something the generator did not already optimize for: a checklist of acceptance criteria, an external check (a unit test, a
tool
result, a retrieved source), or a different model. Self-critique with the same model and prompt tends to rubber-stamp — it shares the generator's blind spots.

items.text: Criteria-based: score the output against an explicit rubric. Cheap, catches omissions and format errors.
Tool-grounded: run a test, re-query a source, or execute the code. Strongest signal, needs an external check to exist.
Cross-model or fresh-context critique: a separate reviewer reduces shared blind spots, at the cost of an extra call.

blocks.title: Design a critique that actually catches errors

spans.text: Before generating, list what a correct output must satisfy — coverage, format, cited claims, no banned actions. The critic scores against this list, not its own taste.

steps.label: Ground the critique externally where you can

spans.text: If a test, schema, or source can check the output, run it and feed the result into the critique. External signal beats the model judging itself.
A useful critique names the specific defect and the fix, so the revise step has something to act on. "Improve clarity" is not actionable; "add a source for the claim about vendor B" is.

blocks.title: Choosing a reflection strategy

options.name: No reflection
options.whenToUse: Use when errors are cheap to spot or cheap to absorb downstream.

options.name: Criteria self-critique

cells.text: Catches omissions and format errors well.
One extra critique call per pass.

options.whenToUse: Use as the default when there is no external check available.

options.name: Tool-grounded reflection

cells.text: Strongest signal — a test or source decides.
Needs a real external check to exist.
Low when the check is trustworthy.

options.whenToUse: Use when output is verifiable: code, math, anything a tool can confirm.

blocks.howToRead: Pick the cheapest strategy whose critique signal is strong enough for the task's error cost. Prefer tool-grounded whenever a real check exists.

blocks.title: Why same-model self-critique rubber-stamps

spans.text: When the same model critiques its own output with no new information, it tends to agree with itself — the critique inherits the same priors that produced the error. This shows up as sycophancy: the reviewer praises plausible-but-wrong work. The fix is to inject information the generator did not have: an external check, a fresh-context reviewer, or a rubric that forces it to look at specific dimensions.
A critique is only worth its cost if it can change the verdict. If it can never say "reject," it is theater — drop it or strengthen the signal.

blocks.prompt: Which reflection setup gives the strongest error signal for an agent writing code?

options.text: Asking the same model "does this look correct?" with the same prompt.
Running the code against a test suite and feeding failures into the critique.
Generating the answer twice and keeping the longer version.

blocks.explanation: Tool-grounded reflection — executing the code and using real test results — provides an external signal the generator cannot rubber-stamp away.

modules.decisionItForces: Choose a reflection strategy for the task: no reflection, criteria self-critique, or tool-grounded reflection, sized to the cost of an error.

modules.title: Wiring them together
modules.sub: Follows m3: combine plan, execute, and reflect into one loop.
modules.summary: A minimal plan-execute-reflect loop in code, with a revision budget so reflection cannot run forever. This module also covers how to verify an AI-written version of this loop before trusting it.
objectives: Trace control flow through a combined plan-execute-reflect loop.
Identify where the revision budget guard must sit to bound reflection.
Verify an AI-generated planning loop before running it.

blocks.title: The combined loop

spans.text: Recall from module 2:
why did we insist the plan live in state rather than only in the prompt?
That same plan-in-state is what the reflect step now reads and rewrites.
Putting it together, one turn of a plan-execute-reflect
agent
looks like: if there is no plan, build one and store it in
state
; otherwise execute the active step, reflect on the result, and either mark the step done or spend a revision from the budget to retry or replan.
The one piece that cannot be skipped is the
revision budget

: a hard cap on how many times reflection may send work back. Without it, a critic that is never satisfied loops forever, burning calls. With it, the loop degrades gracefully — it ships the best attempt when the budget runs out.

blocks.title: Trace one turn of the loop

spans.text: If state holds no plan, call the planner and store the step list. Otherwise find the first step whose status is not done.
Run the active step, then critique its result against the goal. The critique returns pass or fail with a reason.
On pass, mark the step done and move on. On fail, decrement the revision budget and retry or replan — unless the budget is exhausted, in which case ship the best attempt.

blocks.title: Verify an AI-generated planning loop before you trust it

spans.text: When an AI writes this loop for you, check these specific things before running it:

items.text: Is there a hard revision/turn budget, and does the loop actually exit when it hits zero? (The most common bug is an unbounded reflect loop.)
Does the critique have a path to return "fail"? If it can only ever pass, reflection does nothing.
Is the plan stored in state and updated per step, or silently re-derived each turn (which loses progress)?
On budget exhaustion, does it return the best attempt — not crash and not loop?
Are tool calls inside execute guarded for failure, so a bad result becomes a reflectable signal rather than an exception?

blocks.title: Completion problem: the plan-execute-reflect loop
blocks.code:
def run(goal, max_revisions=2):
    plan = make_plan(goal)          # ordered list of steps, stored as state
    for step in plan:
        result = execute(step)
        revisions = 0
        while revisions < max_revisions:
            verdict = reflect(goal, step, result)   # returns ('pass'|'fail', reason)
            if verdict[0] == "pass":
                break
            # TODO: a critique failed and we still have budget.
            #       Spend one revision and produce a new result.
            result = ???
            revisions += 1
        step["output"] = result     # ship best attempt even if budget ran out
    return [s["output"] for s in plan]

spans.text: The plan comes from the planner (module 2); reflect is the critique (module 3). The while loop is the reflection budget guard from this module — it caps retries so a never-satisfied critic cannot loop forever. The missing line must re-do the work using the critique's reason.

predictThenReveal.prompt: Predict the missing line: a critique failed and budget remains. What should `result` become?
predictThenReveal.answer: result = execute(step, feedback=verdict[1]) — re-run the step, passing the critique's reason as feedback so the retry addresses the specific defect rather than blindly repeating.

syntax.explains: Walks the ordered plan one step at a time — this is the planning half.
The reflection budget: bounds how many times a failing step may be retried.
The critique — scores the result against the goal and returns a pass/fail verdict with a reason.
Ships the best attempt even when the budget is exhausted, so the loop degrades gracefully.

blocks.prompt: In the combined loop, what does the revision budget (max_revisions) protect against?

options.text: The plan being stored in state instead of the prompt.
A critic that is never satisfied looping forever and burning calls.
The planner producing steps that are too small.

blocks.explanation: Reflection can reject indefinitely; the budget caps retries so the loop always terminates and ships its best attempt.

modules.title: Where it breaks
modules.sub: Closes the spine: the failure modes and the cost decision.
modules.summary: Planning and reflection have characteristic failure modes — stale plans, runaway reflection, sycophantic self-critique. This module names them, then decides how much of each loop a task actually warrants.
objectives: Name the three failure modes of planning and reflection and how to bound each.
Decide how much planning and reflection a given task warrants.
Recall the plan-execute-reflect loop from memory as a self-check.

blocks.title: How planning and reflection break in practice

spans.text: Both loops fail in characteristic ways. Knowing them is what separates adding these loops by reflex from using them where they pay off.

items.text: Stale plan: the agent commits to a plan-once sequence, the world changes mid-run (a step fails, a price moves), and it keeps executing dead steps. Fix: let reflection invalidate steps and trigger a replan; prefer interleaved replanning in volatile environments.

Runaway reflection: a critic that always finds something to fix loops until the budget runs out, multiplying cost and latency for marginal gains. Fix: a hard revision budget plus a quality threshold — stop when good enough, not when perfect.

Sycophantic self-critique: the same model reviewing its own output rubber-stamps it, so reflection adds cost but catches nothing. Fix: ground the critique in an external check or a fresh-context reviewer.
Over-planning trivial tasks: a one-step task gets a five-step plan and three reflection passes. Fix: gate the loops on task complexity and error cost — most calls should skip both.

blocks.title: Recall the whole loop, then match each failure to its fix

spans.text: Without looking back, name the steps in order: plan, execute, reflect, revise-or-advance. Then say which step the revision budget guards.
Agent drifts off-goal across turns → planning gap. Agent ships confident-but-wrong output → reflection gap. (This is the diagnosis from module 1, now applied to a live trace.)
Stale plan → replan on reflection. Runaway reflection → revision budget. Sycophantic critique → external or fresh-context check. Over-planning → gate on complexity.

blocks.title: How much planning and reflection does this task warrant?

options.name: Neither (reactive)

cells.text: Drifts on long goals; ships unchecked.

options.whenToUse: Use for one-shot lookups and trivial actions where over-engineering costs more than errors.

options.name: Planning only

cells.text: Stays on-goal but still trusts each result.

options.whenToUse: Use when the failure is drift, not correctness — each step is easy to verify on its own.

options.name: Planning + reflection

cells.text: Extra critique and revision calls per step.
Lowest, if reflection is grounded and bounded.

options.whenToUse: Use when both drift and wrong answers are costly — and you can afford the extra calls.

blocks.howToRead: Match the loops to the failure you actually have. Add planning for drift, reflection for correctness; pay for both only when both errors are costly.

blocks.title: Make the loops observable

spans.text: To catch these failures in production, log the plan at creation and after every replan, and log each critique verdict with its reason and the revision count. A trace that shows reflection always passing, or revision counts pinned at the budget cap, is the early warning that the loops are misbehaving.
If you cannot see how many revisions each step took, you cannot tell whether reflection is earning its cost.

blocks.prompt: An agent's traces show every reflection step returning "pass" on the first try, yet users still report wrong answers. What is the likely failure?

options.text: Runaway reflection — the budget is too high.
Sycophantic self-critique — the critic rubber-stamps its own output and needs an external signal.
A stale plan — the plan was built once and never revised.

blocks.explanation: Always-pass critiques with wrong outputs is the signature of self-critique that shares the generator's blind spots; ground it in a test, source, or fresh-context reviewer.

modules.decisionItForces: Decide how much planning and reflection this task warrants: neither, planning only, or both — matched to whether the failure is drift, correctness, or both.

capstone.prompt: Build a plan-execute-reflect agent for a goal of your choice: a planner that writes an ordered plan to state, an executor, and a critique grounded in at least one external check, all bounded by a revision budget. Run it on one task where reflection should reject the first attempt and confirm it revises. NEXT: swap the same-model critic for a fresh-context or cross-model reviewer and measure whether the always-pass rate drops.
